Volume 3: Deep Learning for Researchers

What a neural network is, how it learns, and why deep ones train at all. This volume climbs from the true bottom: one neuron, then a layer, then the forward pass. Then the loss that measures wrongness. Then backpropagation that assigns blame. Then the activations that make depth meaningful.

Only then comes the training-at-scale machinery: optimizers that step wisely, normalization that steadies deep stacks, and initialization that decides the first step. It also covers 16-bit arithmetic that survives and checkpointing that trades compute for memory. Every mechanism is one you will touch when you train at scale in Volume 4.

Assumed known: Volume 1 math, the refresher (which named optimizers, initialization, and normalization without deriving them), and Volume 2's experiment discipline (every lab here reports the same honest way). Forward links: Volume 4 uses pre-norm RMSNorm transformers with BF16 mixed precision; Volume 11 assumes you can read a training curve and diagnose it.

Last verified: September 2026. Live-verified: BatchNorm (Ioffe & Szegedy, ICML 2015, arXiv:1502.03167); LayerNorm (Ba et al., arXiv:1607.06450); RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, NeurIPS 2019, arXiv:1910.07467, 7-64% speedup claim); AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, ICLR 2019, arXiv:1711.05101). Also verified: Xavier init (Glorot & Bengio, AISTATS 2010); He init (He et al., ICCV 2015, arXiv:1502.01852); gradient checkpointing (Chen et al., arXiv:1604.06174). Also verified: BF16 format 1/8/7, max normal 3.38e38 (arXiv:1905.12322); FP16 1/5/10, max 65504 (IEEE 754); PyTorch AMP API (torch.amp.autocast, GradScaler). Every lab number and figure comes from local NumPy runs executed September 2026. UNVERIFIED: none; the memory math in 10.3 is labeled illustrative and uses stated toy-model assumptions.

Chapter 1: The Neuron

Design prompt

  • What is the smallest unit of a neural network that can learn?
  • What does a neuron compute, exactly, in numbers?
  • Why does a neuron need a nonlinearity? What breaks without one?
  • Where does everything a trained network "knows" live?

1.1 What a neuron computes

Step 1: the recipe. A neuron is the smallest learnable unit in a network. It does three things. It multiplies each input by its own weight. A weight is a number the network learns, and it sets how much that input matters.

The neuron adds the results together plus one learned bias. A bias is an offset that shifts the total up or down. Then the neuron passes the sum through an activation function. The activation is a fixed nonlinear function that produces the neuron's output. In symbols:

z = w1x1 + w2x2 + ··· + b,    output = activation(z)

where wi = weight on input i, xi = input i, b = bias (offset)

Step 2: the numbers. Worked example, the neuron in Figure 1.1. Inputs x = [2.0, −1.0, 0.5]. Weights w = [0.8, −0.4, 1.2]. Bias b = 0.3.

z = (2.0)(0.8) + (−1.0)(−0.4) + (0.5)(1.2) + 0.3 = 1.6 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.3 = 2.9
output = ReLU(2.9) = 2.9

ReLU passes positives through unchanged and zeroes negatives

With the ReLU activation (max(0, z), defined properly in Chapter 5), the output is 2.9. Every neuron in every network you will ever train is this computation: multiply, add, bend.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Left: three input circles with their values. Each connecting line carries a weight, written on the line.
  2. Middle: the sum node adds the weighted inputs plus the bias (b = 0.3), giving z = 2.9.
  3. Right: ReLU passes 2.9 through unchanged (it only zeroes negatives). The bottom line shows every multiplication, so you can check the arithmetic by hand.

1.2 Why depth needs the nonlinearity

Step 1: what stacking promises. One neuron draws one decision boundary. Stacking neurons lets the network combine simple boundaries into complex ones. But the combining is done by the activation function, and that is easy to miss.

Step 2: the collapse. Without the activation function, a stack of layers (a layer is simply a group of neurons computed together, formalized in Chapter 2) is just one layer. Two linear layers in a row compute y = W2(W1 x), which equals (W2 W1) x. The product W2 W1 is a single matrix, so the two layers collapse into one. A hundred linear layers have exactly the expressive power of one. Depth without nonlinearity is decoration.

Step 3: the kink. The activation function breaks the collapse by bending the signal. ReLU bends at zero: negatives become zero, positives pass through.

Each neuron contributes one kink. A layer contributes many kinks. The network assembles kinks into curves, and curves into the complex functions that recognize images and language. That is the whole trick of deep learning, and it lives in the activation.

Common misunderstanding: "Deeper is automatically more powerful." Depth only adds power through the nonlinearities. A deep network with no activation functions is a shallow network with extra steps.

"The weighted sum is arithmetic. The nonlinearity is the learning."

1.3 What the weights store

Everything a trained network "knows" lives in its weights and biases. There is no other memory. A large language model is a few hundred billion of these numbers, arranged in layers, each one tuned by training. Training is the project of choosing them.

Every chapter after this one is about choosing them well. Chapter 3 measures how wrong they are. Chapter 4 computes how to fix them. Chapter 6 steps them downhill. Chapters 7 through 10 keep them well-behaved at scale.

Q4. A neuron has inputs x = [1.0, 2.0], weights w = [0.5, -1.0], bias b = 0.5, ReLU activation. Compute z and the output by hand.

Answer: z = (1.0)(0.5) + (2.0)(-1.0) + 0.5 = 0.5 - 2.0 + 0.5 = -1.0. ReLU(-1.0) = 0. The neuron is silent on this input: a negative weighted sum means the evidence points the other way.

Key takeaways

  • A neuron computes z = w.x + b, then applies an activation function. Multiply, add, bend.
  • Weights set how much each input matters; the bias shifts the sum; the activation bends it.
  • Without the nonlinearity, any stack of layers collapses into a single layer.
  • All of a trained network's knowledge lives in its weights and biases. Training chooses them.

Next: Chapter 2 stacks neurons into layers and runs the full forward pass, end to end with numbers.

Chapter 2: Layers and the Forward Pass

Chapter 1 built the smallest learnable unit. One neuron draws one boundary, and real problems need more than one. This chapter stacks neurons into layers and runs the first full forward pass.

Design prompt

  • What does a layer add that a single neuron cannot do?
  • What is a forward pass, exactly?
  • Why is a neural network, computationally, just matrix multiplication?

2.1 From one neuron to a layer

Step 1: many neurons, one input. A layer is many neurons side by side, all reading the same inputs, each with its own weights. Stack the neurons' weight vectors into a matrix W (one row per neuron) and the biases into a vector b, and the whole layer is one line:

z = Wx + b,    activation applied elementwise

where W = weight matrix (one row per neuron), x = input vector, b = bias vector

The network computes all its neurons in parallel because the math is a single matrix operation.

Step 2: hidden layers. A hidden layer is any layer between the input and the output. Its activations (the outputs each neuron produces) are not the answer; they are features the next layer reads. This is where depth earns its keep: each layer re-represents the data, so later layers work with learned features instead of raw inputs. The classic picture: early layers detect edges, middle layers combine edges into shapes, late layers combine shapes into objects.

2.2 The forward pass, end to end

Step 1: the definition. The forward pass is the full computation from input to output. Feed the input into the first layer. Take its activations as the next layer's input. Repeat until the output layer.

This is also what happens at prediction time. Inference means using a trained network to make predictions, and inference is always a forward pass: the same computation, with the weights frozen.

Step 2: the numbers. Worked example, the 3-2-1 network in Figure 2.1. Input x = [1.0, 0.5, -1.0]. Hidden weights W1 = [[0.5, -0.2, 0.3], [0.1, 0.4, -0.5]], biases b1 = [0.1, -0.1].

Hidden neuron 1: z = 0.5(1.0) + (-0.2)(0.5) + 0.3(-1.0) + 0.1. That equals 0.5 - 0.1 - 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.2. ReLU gives 0.2.

Hidden neuron 2: z = 0.1(1.0) + 0.4(0.5) + (-0.5)(-1.0) + (-0.1). That equals 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.5 - 0.1 = 0.7. ReLU gives 0.7.

Output weights W2 = [[0.9, 0.6]], bias b2 = 0.0: z = 0.9(0.2) + 0.6(0.7) + 0.0. That equals 0.18 + 0.42 = 0.6. The network's answer: 0.6.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Left column: the three input values. Every line to the middle column is one weight.
  2. Middle column: the two hidden neurons. The labels show each neuron's weight row and bias, with the resulting z. Both z values are positive, so ReLU passes them through.
  3. Right: the output neuron combines the two hidden activations into 0.6. Follow any path left to right: you trace one term of the matrix multiply.

2.3 Why it is all matrix multiplication

A layer is a matrix-vector product plus an elementwise function. A deep network is a chain of matrix products with kinks between them. That uniformity is the engineering miracle: the entire model reduces to the operation GPUs do fastest. When Volume 15 opens up a GPU kernel, you will see this same z = Wx + b staring back at you. It is also why the field scales by making the matrices bigger: more neurons per layer, more layers, same computation.

Key takeaways

  • A layer is many neurons in parallel: z = Wx + b, activation applied elementwise.
  • Hidden layers re-represent the data; later layers read learned features, not raw inputs.
  • The forward pass chains layers input to output. Inference is a forward pass with frozen weights.
  • The whole network is matrix multiplication, which is why it runs so well on GPUs.

Next: Chapter 3 scores the output: loss functions, and the landscape training walks downhill.

Chapter 3: Loss: How the Network Knows It Is Wrong

The forward pass produces predictions. Nothing so far scores them. This chapter adds the score: the loss function that turns a prediction and its answer into one number, and the landscape that number lives on.

Design prompt

  • What is a loss function, in one sentence?
  • Why do regression and classification use different losses?
  • What does the loss landscape look like, and what is training on it?

3.1 One number for "how wrong"

Step 1: the definition. A loss function turns a prediction and its correct answer into a single number: how wrong the network was on that example. Training is the project of making this number small, on average, across the training data. The loss is the only feedback the network gets.

Step 2: two kinds of answers. Regression means predicting a number (a house price, a temperature). Classification means picking a category (cat or dog, spam or not). They need different losses because "wrong" means different things for a number and a category.

Step 3: mean squared error. For regression, the standard loss is the mean squared error (MSE): the average of (prediction − target) squared.

MSE = (1/n) ∑i (predi − targeti)2

where n = number of examples, predi = prediction on example i, targeti = true answer

Worked example. The network predicts 2.0, the target is 3.0. The error is −1.0. Squared, that is 1.0.

Take three examples. Predictions [2.0, 3.0, 4.0], targets [3.0, 3.0, 6.0]. The squared errors are [1.0, 0.0, 4.0]. The mean is 5/3 ≈ 1.67. Squaring punishes large errors more than small ones, and the loss stays smooth so gradients exist everywhere.

Step 4: cross-entropy. For classification, the standard loss is cross-entropy. The network outputs a probability for the true class, and the loss is minus the log of that probability.

L = −ln(ptrue)

where ptrue = the probability the network assigned to the correct class

Worked example. The network assigns 70% to the correct class, so the loss is −ln(0.7) = 0.357. It assigns 10%: the loss is −ln(0.1) = 2.303. The loss punishes a confident wrong answer far more than an uncertain wrong answer. That steep punishment for confident errors is exactly the pressure that teaches a classifier.

3.2 The loss landscape

Step 1: the picture. The loss landscape is the loss drawn as a function of the weights: a surface with hills and valleys. Each point on the surface is one complete setting of all the weights; its height is the loss. Training walks downhill on this surface. The surface is non-convex (it has many valleys, not one clean bowl), and it lives in millions of dimensions, so the 2D drawing in Figure 3.1 is a cartoon. The cartoon still teaches the right instincts: valleys are good, flat plateaus stall progress, and sharp cliffs punish big steps.

How to read this diagram.
  1. The contours: nested rings of equal loss, like a topographic map. The center is the valley (low loss); the edges are high loss.
  2. The red path: a training run. It starts at random weights (high loss) and each dot is one update step, rolling downhill.
  3. The star: the valley floor the run converges to. Real landscapes have many valleys; the run finds one of them, and in practice that is good enough.

Step 2: why it matters now. Everything from here on is a technique for walking this landscape. The gradient tells you the downhill direction (Chapter 4). The optimizer, the rule that turns gradients into weight updates (Chapter 4; Chapter 6 upgrades it), picks the step. The learning-rate schedule sets the stride (Chapter 6). Volume 11 will teach you to read a training curve the way a doctor reads a chart; the landscape is the anatomy behind it.

Q5. A classifier assigns probability 0.9 to the true class on one example and 0.01 on another. Compute both cross-entropy losses. Which mistake drew the larger penalty, and why is that the right pressure?

Answer: -log(0.9) = 0.105. -log(0.01) = 4.605. The 0.01 mistake draws about 44x the penalty. That is the right pressure. A confident wrong answer means the model's beliefs are badly calibrated. The steep penalty forces the model to fix confident errors first.

Key takeaways

  • A loss function is one number measuring wrongness. Training minimizes it on average.
  • Regression uses mean squared error; classification uses cross-entropy on the true class's probability.
  • Cross-entropy punishes confident wrong answers steeply: -log(0.1) is 2.303, -log(0.7) is 0.357.
  • The loss landscape is the loss as a function of the weights. Training walks it downhill.

Next: Chapter 4 assigns blame: the chain rule, the backward pass, and gradient descent.

Chapter 4: Backpropagation

The loss is one number for the whole network. To improve, the network must blame individual weights: which knob do we turn, and which way? This chapter answers with the chain rule, the backward pass, and gradient descent.

Math prerequisite: this chapter leans on the chain rule and gradients. Full treatment: Vol 1, Ch 4 (chain rule, gradients).

Design prompt

  • How does the network know which weight to blame for an error?
  • What is the chain rule doing inside a network?
  • Why does the gradient computation run backward?
  • What is the training loop, exactly?

4.1 Blame assignment

Step 1: the question. The loss depends on the output. The output depends on the last layer. The last layer depends on the one before it, all the way back to the first weights. To improve one weight, you need one number: how does the loss change when this weight changes a little?

That is a derivative (the slope: how much the output moves per unit change in the input). The gradient is the collection of all these derivatives, one per weight. It points uphill, in the steepest direction. Downhill is the negative gradient.

Step 2: the chain rule. The chain rule splits a derivative through intermediate steps. If the loss L depends on y, and y depends on w:

dL/dw = (dL/dy) · (dy/dw)

where L = loss, y = the neuron's output, w = the weight being blamed

Worked example. The tiny graph from §4.2: x = 2, w = 3, y = w·x = 6, target t = 4, L = (y − t)2 = 4. Then dL/dy = 2(6 − 4) = 4 and dy/dw = x = 2, so dL/dw = 4 · 2 = 8. Each factor is local: dL/dy only involves the loss, dy/dw only involves the neuron. Blame flows backward through the network, one multiplication per hop. That is the entire idea of backpropagation.

4.2 The backward pass, worked

Step 1: the definition. The backward pass, or backpropagation, computes the gradient. It starts at the loss and applies the chain rule layer by layer, back to the first weights. Each layer needs only its own local derivative and the error signal arriving from the layer above. One backward pass yields every weight's gradient at once.

Step 2: the numbers. Worked example, the tiny graph in Figure 4.1. One neuron, no activation: y = w times x, with x = 2 and w = 3. Target t = 4.

  1. Forward. y = w·x = 3·2 = 6. Loss L = (y − t)2 = (6 − 4)2 = 4.
  2. Backward, step 1. dL/dy = 2(y − t) = 2(6 − 4) = 4: how fast the loss moves when the output moves.
  3. Backward, step 2. dy/dw = x = 2: how fast the output moves when the weight moves.
  4. Chain rule. dL/dw = 4 · 2 = 8. The gradient is positive, so w = 3 should decrease (downhill is the negative direction).

A real network is this computation repeated across millions of weights.

Interview signal: be able to run this tiny-graph chain rule by hand: forward values, local derivatives, multiply backward. Interviewers use it to check whether backprop is a memorized phrase or a tool you own.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Top row (blue): the forward pass. x = 2 times w = 3 gives y = 6; the squared error against t = 4 gives L = 4.
  2. Bottom row (red, right to left): the backward pass. It starts with dL/dL = 1 (the loss's derivative with respect to itself), then dL/dy = 4, then dL/dw = 8.
  3. The multiplications: each red step multiplies the incoming error signal by the local derivative (dy/dw = x = 2). That is the chain rule, drawn.

Step 3: why backward, not forward. You could compute each weight's derivative with its own forward pass, but that costs one pass per weight: millions of passes. The backward pass computes all of them in a single sweep, because every weight's chain shares the same downstream factors. Backprop is not a different kind of math; it is the chain rule scheduled in the only order that is affordable.

4.3 Gradient descent: the update

Step 1: the loop. Gradient descent is the training loop: compute the gradient on some data, then step every weight a little downhill:

w ← w − η · dL/dw

where η (eta) = learning rate, the step size; dL/dw = gradient at the current weights

Worked example. Figure 4.2: L = w2, so dL/dw = 2w, with η = 0.3 starting at w = 4.0. Step 1: w = 4.0 − 0.3·8 = 1.6. Step 2: w = 1.6 − 0.3·3.2 = 0.64.

Each step moves against the slope, and the steps shrink as the slope flattens near the bottom. The learning rate sets the step size. Too large, and the steps bounce across the valley or diverge. Too small, and training crawls.

Step 2: the vocabulary of practice. Computing the gradient on the full dataset per step is too slow. Practice uses mini-batches instead: small random subsets of the data, typically tens to thousands of examples. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is gradient descent on mini-batches. Strictly, it means one example at a time. In practice the name covers mini-batches too.

The gradient is noisier, but each step is far cheaper, and the noise turns out to help generalization. One epoch is one full pass over the training data. An optimizer is the rule that turns gradients into weight updates. Plain gradient descent is the simplest optimizer. Chapter 6 upgrades it.

How to read this diagram.
  1. The blue curve: the loss as a function of one weight. The minimum is at w = 0.
  2. The red arrows: three update steps. Each step's length is eta times the local slope, so steps shrink as the slope flattens near the bottom.
  3. The lesson: eta controls everything. The caption's warning is worth memorizing: big eta diverges, small eta crawls.

The three videos at the end of this volume (Watch and go deeper) animate this arc. You will see a network recognize a handwritten digit (the forward pass you just computed). You will see gradient descent walk a loss surface. You will see the update loop worked step by step.

Q6. One neuron: y = w times x, x = 3, w = 2, target t = 10, loss L = (y - t) squared. Compute dL/dw by hand, and say whether w should increase or decrease.

Answer: Forward: y = 6, L = (6 - 10) squared = 16. dL/dy = 2(6 - 10) = -8. dy/dw = x = 3. dL/dw = (-8)(3) = -24. The gradient is negative, so downhill is positive: w should increase.

Key takeaways

  • The gradient is one derivative per weight. It points uphill; training steps the opposite way.
  • The chain rule splits derivatives through intermediate steps: dL/dw = (dL/dy)(dy/dw).
  • Backprop runs the chain rule backward, computing every gradient in one sweep.
  • Gradient descent: w = w - eta times gradient, on mini-batches (SGD), one epoch per full data pass.
  • An optimizer is the rule turning gradients into updates. Plain gradient descent is the simplest one.

Next: Chapter 5 studies the bend: activation functions, and how classifiers turn scores into probabilities.

Chapter 5: Activation Functions

Chapter 1 used ReLU without asking what the options were, or why the bend matters at all. This chapter meets the full cast: sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, and softmax, the function that turns raw scores into probabilities.

Design prompt

  • What does each common activation actually compute?
  • Why is ReLU the default hidden activation?
  • What is a dead ReLU, and what is saturation?
  • How does a classifier turn scores into probabilities?

5.1 The four you will meet

Step 1: the cast. The sigmoid squashes any input into (0, 1). The tanh squashes into (-1, 1). Tanh is zero-centered, so it trains a little better than sigmoid. ReLU (rectified linear unit) is max(0, x): pass positives through, zero out negatives.

For a classifier's output layer, softmax turns a vector of raw scores into probabilities that sum to 1. The raw scores before softmax have a name: logits. Figure 5.1 draws the first three and works a softmax example.

sigmoid(x) = 1 / (1 + e−x)     tanh(x) ∈ (−1, 1)     ReLU(x) = max(0, x)
softmax(z)i = ezi / ∑j ezj

where zi = raw score (logit) for class i; the denominator sums over all classes, so the outputs are probabilities that sum to 1

Worked example. Logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] from Figure 5.1. e2.0 = 7.389, e1.0 = 2.718, e0.1 = 1.105. The sum is 11.212. Probabilities: 7.389 / 11.212 = 0.66, 2.718 / 11.212 = 0.24, 1.105 / 11.212 = 0.10. The biggest logit takes most of the probability, but the others keep a share.

ActivationFormulaOutput rangeDerivativeTypical use
Sigmoid1 / (1 + e−x)(0, 1)s(1 − s); near 0 at extremesGates, binary outputs
Tanh(ex − e−x) / (ex + e−x)(−1, 1)1 − t2; near 0 at extremesHidden layers in older nets
ReLUmax(0, x)[0, ∞)1 if x > 0, else 0Default hidden activation
Softmaxezi / ∑j ezj(0, 1), sums to 1Jacobian, not a scalarClassifier outputs

Step 2: the pairing. Softmax and cross-entropy are a pair: softmax produces the probabilities, cross-entropy scores them. This combination is the standard output of every classifier you will train, including the language models in Volume 4.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Three curves: sigmoid rises from 0 to 1, tanh from -1 to 1, ReLU is flat at zero then a straight line up. All three bend; only ReLU bends sharply.
  2. The notes under each: sigmoid and tanh flatten at the extremes (that flattening is saturation, next section). ReLU's derivative is 1 or 0, nothing in between.
  3. Softmax panel: logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] become [0.66, 0.24, 0.10]. The biggest logit takes most of the probability, but the others keep a share.

5.2 Why ReLU won, and what it costs

Step 1: the win. ReLU's derivative is 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative ones. No squashing, no expensive exponentials, and gradients flow undiminished through active neurons. Sigmoid and tanh saturate: at large positive or negative inputs they flatten out, their derivatives approach zero, and gradients die. In deep stacks that saturation compounds, which is why the field moved hidden layers to ReLU.

Step 2: the cost. A dead ReLU is a neuron whose input is always negative, so its output is always zero and its gradient is always zero. It can never recover: no gradient means no update, which means it stays dead. A few dead neurons are normal and harmless. A layer of them is a corpse. Chapter 8 shows how the initialization scale decides how many neurons die at birth.

Q7. What is the derivative of ReLU at x = 2.5 and at x = -1? If a hidden layer's outputs are all zero on every input, what do you suspect?

Answer: 1 at x = 2.5 (positive side passes through); 0 at x = -1 (negative side is flat). All-zero outputs on all inputs means the ReLUs are dead: their inputs are always negative, so no gradient ever flows. Suspect the initialization scale (Chapter 8).

Key takeaways

  • Sigmoid squashes to (0, 1); tanh to (-1, 1); ReLU is max(0, x); softmax turns logits into probabilities.
  • Softmax plus cross-entropy is the standard classifier output, including for language models.
  • ReLU won because its derivative is 0 or 1: cheap, and gradients flow through active neurons.
  • Saturation (sigmoid/tanh flattening) kills gradients; dead ReLUs (always-negative inputs) never recover.

Next: Chapter 6 upgrades the update rule: momentum, Adam and AdamW, warmup and schedules.

Chapter 6: Optimizers

You can compute gradients now. The next question is what to do with them. Plain gradient descent gives every weight the same step size, which crawls through valleys and bounces across cliffs. This chapter upgrades the update rule: momentum, per-parameter adaptivity, the decoupled weight decay of AdamW, and the schedule that sets the stride.

Design prompt

  • What is Adam doing that SGD is not, in one sentence each for momentum and adaptivity?
  • Why is AdamW different from Adam with weight decay turned on?
  • When would you still pick SGD with momentum over Adam?
  • What is learning-rate warmup, and what breaks without it?

6.1 Adam, decoupled: the AdamW story

Step 1: the two ideas. Adam (the adaptive optimizer that is the default starting point for training neural networks) combines two ideas. Momentum averages past gradients, so consistent directions accelerate and oscillating ones cancel. Adaptive learning rates scale each parameter's step by its historical gradient magnitude: parameters with large, noisy gradients get smaller steps, quiet ones get larger steps. In one sentence: momentum remembers direction, adaptivity normalizes scale.

Step 2: the bug AdamW fixed. In standard Adam, the code implemented "weight decay" as L2 regularization. It added lambda*w to the gradient before the adaptive scaling. The decay term then gets divided by sqrt(v), the adaptive denominator.

Parameters with large gradients get their decay diluted. Parameters with small gradients get it amplified. The effective decay rate varies per parameter and is not the lambda you asked for.

Step 3: the fix. AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, ICLR 2019) decouples it: compute the Adam step from the pure gradient, then shrink the weights directly:

w ← w − η · (m_hat / (√v_hat + ε)) − ηλw

where m_hat = bias-corrected momentum (gradient average), v_hat = bias-corrected squared-gradient average, ε = tiny constant against division by zero, λ = weight-decay strength

Worked example. One weight w = 1.0, with m_hat = 0.5, v_hat = 0.25, η = 0.01, λ = 0.1. Adam step: 0.01 · (0.5 / 0.5) = 0.01. Decay step: 0.01 · 0.1 · 1.0 = 0.001. New weight: 1.0 − 0.01 − 0.001 = 0.989. In Adam with L2 folded into the gradient, the 0.1 penalty would first join the gradient (0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6). Then the adaptive denominator (0.5) would divide it. That gives a distorted step of 0.012 instead of the intended 0.01 plus a separate 0.001.

Every weight decays by exactly ηλ per step, independent of its gradient history. Decoupling separates the optimal weight-decay setting from the learning-rate setting, so you can tune them independently. It substantially improves Adam's generalization. It closes the gap with SGD with momentum on image classification, where Adam had lagged. It is now the default optimizer for transformer training.

Step 4: the numbers. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.3 Part B (same data, same decay 0.1, same 2000 steps; only the placement of the decay differs): Adam with L2 folded into the gradient reaches test MSE 0.2103; AdamW reaches 0.1007. The honest framing, per the paper: this is a generalization win from correct regularization, not a claim about weight norms. Reference: Ilya Loshchilov and Frank Hutter, "Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization," ICLR 2019 (arXiv:1711.05101).

How to read this diagram.
  1. Left (Adam + L2): the narrow "adaptive scale" funnel squeezes the wide "decay" arrow. What comes out is thinner and uneven: parameters with big gradients get less decay.
  2. Right (AdamW): two parallel full-width arrows. The optimizer applies the blue "gradient step" and the teal "decay" independently, so every weight decays by exactly eta times lambda.
  3. The visual moral: coupling the decay to the gradient scale corrupts it. Decoupling restores the intended regularization.

Common misunderstanding: "AdamW just means Adam with weight_decay set." In PyTorch, Adam(weight_decay=...) implements L2-in-the-gradient (the coupled version); AdamW(weight_decay=...) implements the decoupled version. Same argument name, different math. This is exactly the kind of API subtlety design reviews probe.

"Adam with L2 scales your regularization by accident. AdamW applies it on purpose. Same argument name, different math."

Q2. A teammate says AdamW is just Adam with weight decay, so he will use Adam with weight_decay=0.01 and get the same result. What is wrong with that claim? What experiment distinguishes the two?

Answer: Adam's weight_decay adds the penalty to the gradient before adaptive scaling. The effective decay then varies per parameter with gradient history. AdamW applies it after, uniformly. The distinguishing experiment is Lab 3.3 Part B: identical setup, only the placement differs, and AdamW generalizes better (test MSE 0.1007 vs 0.2103).

  • "They are equivalent up to a rescaled lambda," wrong: no single rescaling reproduces per-parameter distortion; the coupling depends on each parameter's gradient history.
  • "The placement relative to the adaptive denominator differs," right: before it (coupled) versus after it (decoupled).

AdamW settles the update rule. What remains is the schedule: how large each step should be over the course of training. Warmup protects the chaotic start; decay squeezes the end.

6.2 Tuning and schedules: warmup and decay

Step 1: the recipe. The learning rate is the most important hyperparameter, and a single constant value is rarely optimal. The standard recipe has two phases. Warmup: start the learning rate near zero and ramp it up over the first few percent of training. Decay: after warmup, anneal it down, most commonly with a cosine schedule that falls smoothly to near zero by the end of training.

Step 2: why warmup exists. At initialization the weights are random. The gradients are large and chaotic. A full learning rate can throw the model into a bad region in the first hundred steps. It can also overflow activations. Warmup lets the statistics (Adam's moments, BatchNorm's running averages) settle before taking full-size steps.

Step 3: why decay helps. Late in training you are near a minimum, and large steps bounce around it. Shrinking the step size squeezes out the last quality. The cosine schedule's shape matters less than its endpoints. What counts is this: start small, spend most of training at a productive middle rate, and finish small. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.3 Part A (ill-conditioned quadratic, 500 steps): SGD reaches 2.3e-2, SGD with momentum 3.9e-14, Adam 1.9e-20, AdamW 4.2e-3.

Note AdamW looks worst here. Weight decay is a regularizer, and on a pure optimization problem with no overfitting, regularization only hurts. That is not a contradiction.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Loss curves: plain SGD crawls (2.3e-2); momentum accelerates through the valley (3.9e-14); Adam's per-parameter scaling wins outright (1.9e-20). AdamW trails because decay penalizes the optimum on a problem with nothing to regularize.
  2. Schedule: the learning rate ramps linearly from zero (warmup), holds, then follows a cosine down to near zero. The shape is the standard recipe: protect the start, squeeze the end.
  3. Read the two panels together: the optimizer picks the step direction; the schedule picks the step size over time. You need both.

Common misunderstanding: "Adam needs no tuning." Adam still has a learning rate, betas, epsilon, and (in AdamW) a weight decay that interacts with the learning rate. Defaults are where you start, not the answer.

"Warmup protects the chaotic start; cosine decay squeezes the end. The schedule is half the optimizer."

Learning-rate schedule: warmup + cosine decay
================================================
 lr ^
    |         ****
    |       **    ***
    |     **         ****
    |   **               *****
    | **                      *********
    +----------------------------------> steps
      warmup       cosine decay to ~0

Warmup: ramp from near zero over the first few percent of steps.
Why: random init plus large chaotic gradients plus unsettled
Adam moments means a full step can wreck the first 100 steps.
Decay: finish small, so late steps squeeze out the last quality.

6.3 Lab 3.3: the optimizer laboratory

Lab 3.3: optimizers (labs/lab_3_3_optimizers.py)

Two parts. Part A races SGD, SGD with momentum, Adam, and AdamW on an ill-conditioned quadratic (a valley 100x steeper in one direction). Part B isolates the AdamW question: same data, same weight decay, same steps; only the placement of the decay differs.

Captured output (verbatim):

Part A: final loss after 500 steps (ill-conditioned quadratic)
  sgd            lr=0.0015  final loss 2.338e-02
  sgd+momentum   lr=0.002   final loss 3.912e-14
  adam           lr=0.05    final loss 1.868e-20
  adamw          lr=0.05    final loss 4.200e-03

Part B: same data, same wd=0.1, same 2000 steps.
Only the placement of the decay differs.
  adam + L2 in grad    ||w||=2.645  train MSE=0.1741  TEST MSE=0.2103
  adamw (decoupled)    ||w||=2.968  train MSE=0.0852  TEST MSE=0.1007
  AdamW wins on test error: the L2 gradient folded into Adam
  pollutes the momentum/second-moment estimates and gets divided
  by the adaptive denominator, so it regularizes unevenly.

Read Part A as an optimization story and Part B as a generalization story. They answer different questions, and conflating them is how optimizer myths start.

Key takeaways

  • Adam = momentum plus per-parameter adaptive scaling.
  • AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive update; Adam's weight_decay does not.
  • Warmup protects early training; cosine decay finishes it. Tune the schedule, not just the optimizer.
  • Judge optimizers on generalization (Part B), not just loss curves (Part A).

Next: Chapter 7 keeps the signal well-behaved through deep stacks: normalization.

Chapter 7: Normalization

You have now trained a network in your head: neuron, layer, forward pass, loss, backprop, activations, optimizer. Everything so far assumed the signals stay well-behaved through dozens of layers. They do not. As signals flow through a deep stack, their scale drifts: activations grow or shrink, gradients follow, and training stalls or explodes. Normalization is the fix. It re-centers and re-scales the activations at every layer, so each layer always receives well-behaved inputs.

Design prompt

  • Why do deep stacks need normalization at all?
  • Batch normalization vs layer normalization: what axis is different?
  • Why do transformers use LayerNorm and RMSNorm instead of BatchNorm?
  • Pre-norm vs post-norm: where does the norm sit, and why does it matter?

7.1 BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm: three answers to one problem

Step 1: the problem. As signals flow through many layers, their scale drifts. Activations grow or shrink, gradients follow, and training stalls or explodes. Normalization re-centers and re-scales activations so each layer receives well-behaved inputs. The three classic methods differ in one choice: which axis you compute the statistics over.

Step 2: the three methods. Batch normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy, ICML 2015) normalizes each feature across the batch. For every channel, subtract the batch mean and divide by the batch standard deviation. Then apply a learned scale and shift.

At test time there is no batch, so it uses running averages collected during training. Layer normalization (Ba et al., 2016) normalizes across the features of each single example instead. No batch dependence, identical behavior in train and test.

RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, NeurIPS 2019) drops the mean subtraction and the bias. It divides by the root-mean-square only. The authors showed the re-scaling does the work and the re-centering is dispensable. That cuts 7-64% of the normalization cost across their experiments.

x̂ = (x − μ) / √(σ2 + ε),    y = γx̂ + β

where μ = mean, σ2 = variance, ε = tiny constant, γ = learned scale, β = learned shift; BatchNorm takes μ, σ2 over the batch, LayerNorm over the example's features

Worked example. One feature with values [2, 4, 6]. μ = 4. σ2 = ((−2)2 + 02 + 22) / 3 = 8/3 ≈ 2.667. σ ≈ 1.633. Normalized: [(2−4)/1.633, (4−4)/1.633, (6−4)/1.633] = [−1.22, 0, 1.22]. With γ = 1 and β = 0 the output is the normalized values themselves. The axis you average over is the only difference between the methods.

MethodStatistics computed overTest-time behaviorNote
BatchNormEach feature, across the batchRunning averages collected during trainingBatch statistics get noisy with small batches
LayerNormEach example, across its featuresSame as training (batch-free)Transformers' choice for sequences
RMSNormEach example, across its featuresSame as training (batch-free)No mean step; cheaper (7-64% of norm cost cut)

Step 3: why it helps, honestly. The story has evolved. The original BatchNorm paper blamed internal covariate shift (drifting input distributions at each layer). Later work (Santurkar et al., NeurIPS 2018) argued the bigger effect is a smoother optimization landscape.

Normalization reparameterizes the problem. Gradients become better behaved, and larger learning rates work. Either way, the practical effect is the same: deeper nets train, faster, with less fuss about initialization and learning rate.

Step 4: the numbers. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.1 (16-layer MLP, 300 steps). No normalization stalls at loss 3.33. Batch normalization reaches 1.33. Layer normalization reaches 2.65. RMSNorm reaches 2.65.

One honest note: on this toy, BatchNorm wins outright. LayerNorm's advantages are regime-specific: small batches, sequences, and transformers, where batch statistics are noisy or meaningless. The lab is honest about that instead of pretending one method always wins.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Picture activations as a grid: rows are batch examples, columns are features.
  2. BatchNorm computes statistics down each column (across examples). The statistics change with every batch, which is why test time needs running averages.
  3. LayerNorm computes statistics across each row (across features of one example). Batch size is irrelevant, so train and test behave identically.
  4. The worked numbers show the same normalize-then-scale-and-shift recipe applied on the two different axes.

Common misunderstanding: "BatchNorm is always best because it won the toy shootout." BatchNorm's batch statistics get noisy with small batches. Single-example inference has no batch statistics at all. That is why transformers, with their variable-length sequences, standardized on LayerNorm and RMSNorm instead.

"Normalization is not one method; it is one recipe applied on different axes. The axis decides where it works."

Q1. You switch a BatchNorm model from training to evaluation and accuracy collapses, but only with batch size 1. What broke, and what is the one-line conceptual fix?

Answer: at test time BatchNorm uses running averages, not batch statistics. Batch size 1 alone cannot break it. The collapse means the model was accidentally left in training mode. It can also mean the running averages were never updated. Conceptually: call eval mode so the network uses the frozen running statistics.

  • "BatchNorm cannot work with batch size 1," wrong: inference uses running averages, which are batch-size independent. The failure is a mode bug, not a math limit.
  • "The layer was still normalizing with batch statistics," right: train/test behavior differs by design; eval mode is the switch.
The three norms: which axis gets averaged
================================================
BatchNorm : each feature, ACROSS the batch (down a column)
LayerNorm : each example, ACROSS its features (across a row)
RMSNorm   : each example, ACROSS its features, no mean step

Why transformers pick LayerNorm:
  the batch axis breaks for sequences (variable lengths,
  one token at a time at inference). Per-example statistics
  do not care about the batch at all.

You have settled the axis question. Now the placement question: inside a transformer block, where does the normalization sit relative to the skip connection? The answer decides how gradients flow through depth.

7.2 Pre-norm vs post-norm: where the norm sits

Step 1: the two layouts. In a transformer block the normalization can sit in two places. Post-norm (the original Transformer layout) applies the norm after the residual addition: x + Sublayer(x), then normalize. Pre-norm normalizes before the sublayer, inside the residual branch: x + Sublayer(Norm(x)). Same components, different order, very different training dynamics.

Step 2: why pre-norm trains easier. In post-norm, the residual stream passes through a normalization at every layer. The signal gets repeatedly re-scaled. Gradients must flow through each norm on the main path. Deep post-norm stacks are finicky: they often need learning-rate warmup and careful initialization to get going.

In pre-norm, the residual stream is a clean highway. The identity path carries gradients straight through all layers. Each sublayer only has to learn a perturbation of an already-normalized input. The result is dramatically more stable training, which is why essentially every modern LLM uses pre-norm.

Step 3: the honest tradeoff. When post-norm does train successfully, it can reach slightly better final quality. The normalization on the main path keeps representations tighter. Pre-norm trades a little of that ceiling for a much wider stable region.

The field chose pre-norm because at LLM scale, reliably finishing training beats maybe finishing slightly better. Stability is the feature. The last half point of quality is the price.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Post-norm (left): input flows down through Add then Norm. The curved skip arrow joins before the norm, so the norm re-normalizes every layer's output, including the accumulated residual signal.
  2. Pre-norm (right): Norm comes first, then the MLP, then the Add. The skip arrow carries the raw signal straight through, untouched by any normalization.
  3. Follow the gradient backward: in pre-norm it rides the clean skip path through all layers. That unobstructed highway is the stability story.

"Pre-norm keeps the residual stream a clean highway. Stability is the feature; the last half point of quality is the price."

7.3 Lab 3.1: the normalization shootout

Lab 3.1: normalization shootout (labs/lab_3_1_normalization.py)

A 16-layer MLP trained 300 steps four ways: no normalization, batch normalization, layer normalization, RMSNorm. The lab gradient-checks all backward passes to 1e-9, so the differences are the methods, not bugs.

Captured output (verbatim):

none       final loss 3.3332 (started 3.5382)
batchnorm  final loss 1.3276 (started 3.4477)
layernorm  final loss 2.6461 (started 3.4404)
rmsnorm    final loss 2.6521 (started 3.4579)
took 123.4s
How to read this diagram.
  1. Four loss curves over 300 steps, same network, same data. Only the normalization differs.
  2. The gray curve (none) is nearly flat: the signal degrades through 16 unnormalized layers and gradients cannot do their job.
  3. All three normalized curves fall. BatchNorm falls fastest here because the batch statistics are clean on this toy; LayerNorm and RMSNorm tie at 2.65.
  4. The honest reading: normalization carries the load, and the winner depends on the regime, not on a universal ranking.

Key takeaways

  • Normalization controls activation scale; the axis (batch vs features) defines the method.
  • BatchNorm: batch statistics, needs running averages at test. LayerNorm: per-example, batch-free. RMSNorm: scale-only, cheaper.
  • Pre-norm stabilizes deep transformers by keeping the residual stream clean.
  • No universal winner: match the method to the regime (batch size, sequences, inference).

Next: Chapter 8 fixes the start: initialization scales that keep signals alive through depth.

Chapter 8: Initialization

Normalization steadies the signal during training. It cannot fix a dead start. Before the first gradient step, the weights are random numbers, and their scale decides whether any signal survives the forward pass at all. Choose badly and the network is a corpse before training begins. This chapter is about choosing well.

Design prompt

  • Why can you not initialize all weights to zero?
  • What goes wrong with N(0,1) weights in a 30-layer network?
  • Why does ReLU need a different scale than tanh?
  • How do you diagnose a dead network at initialization?

8.1 The variance problem: signals compound through depth

Step 1: why not zero. Zero initialization fails for a simple reason: every neuron computes the same thing, gets the same gradient, and updates identically forever. Symmetry never breaks. So we initialize randomly, but the scale of the randomness decides whether the network can learn at all.

Step 2: the compounding. Variances multiply through layers. For one layer, Var(z) = fan_in times Var(w) times Var(x). Fan_in is the number of inputs to a neuron. Each output sums fan_in terms, each contributing Var(w)*Var(x). If Var(w) = 1 and fan_in = 512, every layer multiplies the variance by 512.

After 10 layers the signal has grown by 512^10, about 1.2e27: pure explosion. If Var(w) is too small, the signal shrinks geometrically instead: vanishing. Either way, by layer 30 the activations are all enormous or all zero. The gradients follow them, and training never starts.

Step 3: the numbers. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.2 (30-layer ReLU network, activation variance measured at layer 1 and layer 30): N(0,1) grows from 43.8 to 1.48e+54 (explosion). N(0,0.02) shrinks from 0.0175 to 1.00e-30 (vanishing). Both are dead before the first gradient step.

How to read this diagram.
  1. The x-axis is layer depth (1 to 30); the y-axis is activation variance on a log scale. Flat is healthy.
  2. Too big (red) climbs to 1e54: explosion. Too small (gray) falls to 1e-30: vanishing. Both networks are untrainable.
  3. Xavier (amber) decays slowly: Glorot and Bengio derived it for symmetric activations, and ReLU's one-sidedness breaks its assumption.
  4. He (teal) stays near 1.0 across all 30 layers. That flat line is the entire point of the next section.

Common misunderstanding: "Small random values are always safe." Too small is exactly as fatal as too big. The signal vanishes geometrically and gradients die with it. Safety is not smallness. It is the right scale for the activation.

"Variance compounds multiplicatively through depth. The initialization scale is not a detail; it is the difference between a network and a random number generator."

30-layer ReLU net: variance at layer 1 -> layer 30
========================================================
init N(0, 1)     : 43.8     -> 1.48e+54    EXPLODES
init N(0, 0.02)  : 0.0175   -> 1.00e-30    VANISHES
He init          : ~1       -> ~1          survives

Rule of thumb: Var(w) = 2 / fan_in for ReLU (He).
Each layer multiplies variance by fan_in * Var(w).
Choose Var(w) so the product stays 1.

8.2 Xavier and He, derived

Step 1: the goal and the symmetric case. Choose Var(w) so the signal variance stays constant through every layer, forward and backward. Xavier initialization (Glorot & Bengio, AISTATS 2010) solves this for symmetric activations like tanh and sigmoid. These activations are roughly linear near zero at initialization.

The solution: Var(w) = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out). Use uniform weights in [-sqrt(6/(fan_in+fan_out)), +sqrt(6/(fan_in+fan_out))]. Or use normal weights with std sqrt(2/(fan_in+fan_out)).

Step 2: the ReLU correction. He initialization (He et al., ICCV 2015) fixes the rule for ReLU. ReLU zeroes out roughly half its inputs, which halves the variance surviving each layer (E[ReLU(x)^2] = Var(x)/2 for symmetric x). The correction is a factor of 2: Var(w) = 2 / fan_in, i.e. weights drawn normal with std sqrt(2/fan_in). Doubling the weight variance restores the balance.

Step 3: the lab confirms the theory. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.2. Xavier's variance decays from 0.341 at layer 1 to 6.10e-10 at layer 30. That matches the theory for ReLU exactly: the missing factor of 2 compounds into slow decay. He holds 0.685 to 0.965: flat.

References. Xavier Glorot and Yoshua Bengio, "Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks," AISTATS 2010. Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun, "Delving Deep into Rectifiers: Surpassing Human-Level Performance on ImageNet Classification," ICCV 2015 (arXiv:1502.01852).

Derivation trace (one layer, ReLU, fan_in = n)
================================================
 z = w1*x1 + ... + wn*xn,  wi ~ N(0, s^2), xi symmetric, Var(x)=v
 Var(z) = n * s^2 * v            (sum of n independent terms)
 a = ReLU(z): E[a^2] = Var(z)/2  (half the mass is zeroed)
 Want Var(a) = v  =>  n * s^2 * v / 2 = v  =>  s^2 = 2/n
 => He:  w ~ N(0, sqrt(2/fan_in))
 For tanh (no zeroing): s^2 = 1/fan_in; averaging forward and
 backward constraints gives Xavier: s^2 = 2/(fan_in + fan_out).
================================================
Worked example, fan_in = 512, fan_out = 512:
 Xavier std = sqrt(2/1024) = 0.0442
 He std     = sqrt(2/512)  = 0.0625   (larger: compensates ReLU)

Concrete numbers from Lab 3.2. Xavier's variance decays from 0.341 at layer 1 to 6.10e-10 at layer 30. That matches the theory for ReLU: the missing factor of 2 compounds into slow decay. He holds 0.685 to 0.965: flat. The lab confirms the derivation, including Xavier's predicted failure mode on ReLU.

References. Xavier Glorot and Yoshua Bengio, "Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks," AISTATS 2010. Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, Jian Sun, "Delving Deep into Rectifiers: Surpassing Human-Level Performance on ImageNet Classification," ICCV 2015 (arXiv:1502.01852).

"Xavier preserves variance through symmetric activations; He adds the factor of 2 that ReLU's zeroing demands."

8.3 Dead networks and diagnosis

Step 1: what "dead" means. A dead ReLU is a neuron whose input is always negative. Its output is always zero and its gradient is always zero. It can never recover.

A few dead neurons are normal (ReLU zeroes about half its inputs at initialization with symmetric data). A network where most neurons are dead, or where whole layers output zeros, is a corpse: no gradient flows, no learning happens. Luck produces a few dead neurons; a bad initialization scale produces layers of them systematically.

Step 2: the cheap diagnosis. Forward one batch at initialization and check per-layer statistics. Healthy signs: activation variance near 1.0 and roughly half the ReLUs active. Warning signs: variance at 1e-30 or 1e54 (see Figure 8.1), or entire layers with zero variance. Lab 3.2 measured dead fractions at layer 30: 41.6% for the too-big, too-small, and He initializations (near the expected ~50% for ReLU), and 53.6% for Xavier. The dead fraction alone does not diagnose; the variance trajectory does.

Step 3: the field habit. Engineers who have debugged real training runs put it like this. "Before training, I forward a batch and check per-layer activation mean, variance, and dead fraction. If the variance is not order-1 by layer 10, I fix the initialization before burning GPU hours."

How to read this diagram.
  1. Three columns of neurons with connections between them. Blue neurons are alive; gray neurons are dead.
  2. Each dead neuron carries a small "0": its output is exactly zero for every input, so its gradient is zero too.
  3. The faded outgoing lines show the consequence: downstream neurons lose those inputs permanently. Dead neurons never revive, so check at initialization.

8.4 Lab 3.2: the initialization sweep

Lab 3.2: initialization (labs/lab_3_2_initialization.py)

A 30-layer ReLU network, four initializations. Forward one batch at initialization and measure activation variance at layer 1 and layer 30, plus the dead-neuron fraction at layer 30.

init N(0, 1)    : variance 43.8   -> 1.48e+54   EXPLODES,    dead 41.6%
init N(0, 0.02) : variance 0.0175 -> 1.00e-30   VANISHES,    dead 41.6%
Xavier          : variance 0.341  -> 6.10e-10   slow decay,  dead 53.6%
He              : variance 0.685  -> 0.965      flat,        dead 41.6%

The dead fraction alone does not diagnose: all four sit near 40-55% (ReLU zeroes about half its inputs by symmetry). The variance trajectory does. Only He keeps the signal order-1 across all 30 layers, which is why the network trains.

Key takeaways

  • Zero init never breaks symmetry; random init needs exactly the right scale.
  • Variance compounds multiplicatively: too big explodes, too small vanishes.
  • Xavier (2/(fan_in+fan_out)) for symmetric activations; He (2/fan_in) for ReLU.
  • Diagnose before training: forward a batch, check per-layer variance and dead fraction.

Next: Chapter 9 spends bits where they matter: mixed-precision training in 16 bits.

Chapter 9: Mixed Precision

The network trains now. It is just slow and memory-hungry, because every number so far has been a 32-bit float. Modern hardware computes faster in 16 bits and moves half the bytes. This chapter is about spending bits where they matter: 16-bit compute, with 32-bit precision kept exactly where the math needs it.

Design prompt

  • Why train in 16 bits at all? What do you gain?
  • FP16 vs BF16: what is the actual tradeoff, in bits?
  • What breaks in FP16, and how does loss scaling fix it?
  • Why do the master weights live in FP32?

9.1 FP16 vs BF16: range against precision

Step 1: why 16 bits. Mixed precision training keeps master weights and sensitive operations in FP32 but runs the heavy compute (matrix multiplications, activations) in 16 bits. The gain: half the memory traffic and, on tensor-core hardware, multiples of the throughput. The cost: 16 bits cannot represent everything, and the two 16-bit formats fail in opposite ways.

Step 2: the formats, in bits. FP16 (IEEE 754 half precision): 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits. Range: max normal 65,504, min normal 6.10e-5. BF16 (bfloat16): 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 7 mantissa bits. Range: max normal 3.38e38, min normal 1.17e-38, the same range as FP32. The tradeoff is exact: FP16 spends its bits on precision (10 mantissa bits, ~3-4 decimal digits) and starves the exponent; BF16 keeps FP32's full 8-bit exponent and sacrifices mantissa (7 bits, ~2-3 digits).

Step 3: why range beats precision in training. Gradients routinely live at 1e-6 to 1e-8; in FP16 anything below 6.1e-5 flushes to zero and the signal dies silently. Activations and logits routinely exceed 65,504; in FP16 they overflow to infinity. BF16 survives both because its exponent matches FP32. Fewer mantissa bits do not make BF16 worse for training; they make it coarser where coarseness is harmless. That is why modern LLM training standardized on BF16: you lose precision you did not need and keep range you cannot live without.

Step 4: the numbers. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.4. 1e5 in FP16 overflows to inf. In simulated BF16 it rounds to 9.984e4. 1e30 in FP16 is inf. In BF16 it is 9.953e29.

Near 1.0, adding 0.001: FP32 gives 1.001000, FP16 gives 1.000977, BF16 rounds back to 1.000000 (its spacing near 1.0 is 2^-8). BF16 is coarser near 1.0 and infinitely more capable at the extremes. Reference: "A Study of BFLOAT16 for Deep Learning Training" (arXiv:1905.12322) gives the format table. FP32 1/8/23 max 3.40e38. FP16 1/5/10 max 6.55e4. BFLOAT16 1/8/7 max 3.38e38.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Three bars: FP32 (32 bits), BF16 (16 bits), FP16 (16 bits). Each bar is split into sign (navy), exponent (blue), mantissa (teal).
  2. Compare the blue segments: FP32 and BF16 both have 8 exponent bits (same range, ~1e38); FP16 has only 5 (max 65,504).
  3. Compare the teal segments: FP16 has the most mantissa (10 bits, finest near 1.0); BF16 has the least (7 bits). Precision versus range, made visible.

"FP16 buys precision and starves range; BF16 keeps FP32's range and spends precision. Training needs range."

16-bit float layouts (1 sign bit each)
================================================
FP16:  s | eeeee | mmmmmmmmmm        1-5-10
       sign  5-bit exp   10-bit mantissa
       range: 6.10e-5 .. 65,504 (normals)

BF16:  s | eeeeeeee | mmmmmmm         1-8-7
       sign  8-bit exp   7-bit mantissa
       range: 1.17e-38 .. 3.38e38 (normals, = FP32)

FP16 buys precision and starves range.
BF16 keeps FP32's range and spends less on precision.
Gradients live at 1e-6 to 1e-8: FP16 flushes them to
zero, BF16 represents them fine.

9.2 Loss scaling: rescuing the small gradients

Step 1: the underflow problem. FP16's narrow range creates the underflow problem. Gradients smaller than ~6.1e-5 round to exactly zero. The network stops learning in its deepest layers first. Loss scaling is the fix.

Multiply the loss by a large scale S before backpropagation. That shifts every gradient up by S into FP16's representable range. Then divide the gradients by S before the optimizer step. The math cancels exactly. Only the representable window moves. It does not change what the model learns.

Step 2: the protocol. Three steps, plus one rule. This is dynamic loss scaling, and it is what PyTorch's GradScaler implements.

  1. Multiply the loss by S.
  2. Run the backward pass in FP16.
  3. Divide the gradients by S, then run the optimizer step.

The rule: if any gradient overflows to inf or NaN, skip that optimizer step entirely and shrink S. If many steps are clean, grow S for more headroom. If scaled gradients still underflow, the scale was too small. The idea is not wrong.

In code: scaler.scale(loss).backward(), then scaler.step(optimizer) and scaler.update(). With BF16, you need none of this. The exponent range already matches FP32. The standard recipe is torch.amp.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) with no scaler at all.

Step 3: the numbers. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.4: a true gradient of 1.0e-8 becomes exactly 0.0 in FP16 (far below the 6.1e-5 minimum normal). With loss scale 1024, the hardware stores it as 1.025e-5, safely representable, and unscales back to 1.0e-8. Rescued, bit for bit in effect.

gtrue = (S · gtrue) / S

where S = loss scale; the math cancels exactly, only the representable window moves

Worked example. True gradient g = 1.0e-8, far below FP16's 6.1e-5 floor. Scale: 1.0e-8 · 1024 = 1.024e-5, stored as 1.025e-5, safely representable. Unscale: 1.025e-5 / 1024 ≈ 1.0e-8. Nothing was lost; the window moved.

Step 4: the second half of the recipe. The master weights stay in FP32. A weight update of 1e-6 applied to a weight stored in FP16 near 1.0 would round to nothing. FP16's spacing there is ~1e-3. The update vanishes and training stalls.

The pattern is this. Do the forward and backward passes in 16 bits. Keep an FP32 copy of the weights. Apply the update to the FP32 copy, then cast down for the next step. Lab 3.4 section 4 shows the stuck-weight failure directly.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Loss (navy): the code multiplies it by 1024. The arrow label is the scale factor S.
  2. Backward in FP16 (teal): every gradient is 1024x larger than its true value, sitting safely above the underflow floor. The growing bar shows the shift into representable range.
  3. Gradients (blue): the code divides them by 1024 back to true scale. Then the Update in FP32 (navy) applies them to the master weights. The stable bar shows nothing was lost.

"Loss scaling does not change the math; it moves the math into a window FP16 can see. BF16 skips the whole dance."

Q3. Training in FP16 with a fixed loss scale of 65536 diverges with NaNs halfway through. Your fix options: (A) raise the scale, (B) lower the scale, (C) switch to BF16. Which and why?

Answer: B first, C if the hardware allows. NaNs mean overflow: gradients hit FP16's ceiling, so the scale is too large and must come down. Dynamic scaling does this automatically, skipping the corrupted step. Switching to BF16 removes the need for scaling entirely on supported hardware.

  • A, wrong: raising the scale makes overflow worse; the scale was already too aggressive.
  • B, right: overflow calls for a smaller scale, exactly what dynamic scaling does on detecting inf/NaN.
  • C, right: BF16's FP32-sized range eliminates both overflow and underflow concerns.
Loss scaling: move the window, keep the math
====================================================
grad (true)      in FP16          x S=32768       in FP16
1.0e-8     ->    0.0 (underflow)  3.3e-4          representable

The pipeline:
  loss * S  ->  backward (FP16)  ->  grads / S  ->  optimizer step
The math cancels exactly; only the representable window moves.

The rule:
  any grad overflows to inf/NaN -> skip the step, shrink S
  many clean steps              -> grow S for more headroom
This is dynamic loss scaling (PyTorch GradScaler).
BF16 needs none of this: its exponent already matches FP32.

9.3 Lab 3.4: the numerics laboratory

Lab 3.4: mixed-precision numerics (labs/lab_3_4_mixed_precision.py)

The lab simulates BF16 by truncating FP32 mantissas (no torch needed). It runs four experiments: range, precision, underflow with loss scaling, and stuck weights. Captured output (verbatim, abridged):

1. RANGE: what each format can represent
  float32                1e+05 -> 1.000e+05
  float32                1e+30 -> 1.000e+30
  bfloat16 (simulated)   1e+05 -> 9.984e+04
  bfloat16 (simulated)   1e+30 -> 9.953e+29
  float16                1e+05 -> inf   OVERFLOW
  float16                1e+30 -> inf   OVERFLOW

2. PRECISION: what each format can resolve near 1.0
1.0 + 0.001 (does the addition survive?)
  float32                            1.001000
  bfloat16                           1.000000  <- rounds back to 1.0 (spacing near 1.0 is 2^-8)
  float16                            1.000977

3. UNDERFLOW: the small-gradient problem, and loss scaling
  true gradient .................. 1.0e-08
  in float16 ..................... 0.0e+00  <- rounds to ZERO
  (fp16 min normal = 6.1e-05; 1e-8 is far below it)
  with loss scale 1024: stored 1.025e-05, unscaled back to 1.0e-08  <- rescued

4. STUCK WEIGHTS: why the master copy lives in FP32
  (weight update smaller than the fp16 spacing near 1.0 rounds to
   nothing; the fp32 master copy accumulates it correctly)

The lab's moral in one line: FP16 fails at the extremes, BF16 fails near 1.0, and training lives at the extremes.

Key takeaways

  • Mixed precision: 16-bit compute, FP32 master weights, sensitive ops in FP32.
  • FP16: 1/5/10, max 65,504, needs loss scaling. BF16: 1/8/7, FP32-sized range, usually needs no scaling.
  • Loss scaling shifts gradients into the representable window and cancels exactly.
  • PyTorch: torch.amp.autocast plus GradScaler for FP16; autocast with BF16 and no scaler otherwise.

Next: Chapter 10 trades compute for memory: gradient checkpointing.

Chapter 10: Gradient Checkpointing

Precision cut the bytes per number. The remaining problem is the count of numbers. At long sequences, the activations saved for the backward pass dwarf the weights. This chapter trades compute for memory: deliberately forget most activations, then recompute them when the backward pass needs them.

Design prompt

  • During training, what eats more memory: weights or activations?
  • What is gradient checkpointing in one sentence?
  • What is the exact tradeoff: how much memory for how much compute?
  • What does checkpointing not save?

10.1 The memory wall: activations dominate

Step 1: what eats the memory. Backpropagation needs values from the forward pass. Autograd therefore saves activations. It saves every layer's inputs, normalization statistics, and attention scores. Attention scores come from the attention mechanism, introduced in Chapter 11. Autograd holds them until the backward pass consumes them.

In a deep network these saved tensors routinely exceed the weights. The memory grows with layers times sequence length times batch size times hidden size. At long sequences it is the activations, not the parameters, that kill the job.

Step 2: the accounting. Per layer: input activations (batch * seq * hidden * bytes), attention scores (batch * heads * seq * seq * bytes, unless the code uses FlashAttention (an IO-aware attention implementation that avoids materializing the full score matrix)), MLP intermediates (several multiples of the hidden size), plus normalization copies. Multiply by layer count. The weights, by contrast, enter the count once. This is why a 7B-parameter model in FP16 needs ~14 GB for weights but can need 5x that in activations at long context.

Step 3: the numbers. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.5 (illustrative model: 24 layers, hidden 1024, sequence 2048, batch 8, FP16): storing everything costs 36.24 GB of activation memory without FlashAttention, 10.47 GB with it. The lab labels these illustrative tensor counts; the point is the ratio between strategies, which stays stable.

Activation memory accounting (lab 3.5 model, per strategy)
======================================================================
FlashAttention OFF (attention scores materialized):
  activation bytes per layer: 1.51 GB
  store everything ............ 36.24 GB   1.00x compute
  checkpoint every 4 layers ...  6.24 GB   ~1.33x compute   (5.8x less)

FlashAttention ON (no s-by-s matrix stored):
  activation bytes per layer: 0.44 GB
  store everything ............ 10.47 GB   1.00x compute
  checkpoint every 4 layers ...  1.95 GB   ~1.33x compute   (5.4x less)
======================================================================
Illustrative tensor counts; the ratio between strategies is the lesson.

Common misunderstanding: "Checkpointing reduces optimizer memory." It does not. Parameters, gradients, and optimizer state stay untouched. Checkpointing attacks saved activations only. If your job dies from Adam's state, you need sharding (splitting optimizer state across GPUs) or offloading (parking it in CPU memory), not checkpointing.

"At long sequences, activations dwarf weights. Budget the activations first."

Memory, Lab 3.5 (24 layers, d=1024, seq 2048, batch 8, FP16)
========================================================================
weights (FP16)            ~14 GB    [########               ]
activations, no FlashAttn ~36 GB    [########################]
activations, FlashAttn    ~10 GB    [######                 ]

Activations grow with layers x seq x batch x hidden.
At long context they dwarf the weights. That is why
checkpointing trades compute for memory.

10.2 The tradeoff: forget and recompute

Step 1: the trade. Gradient checkpointing (also called activation checkpointing) trades compute for memory. Save only every k-th layer's activations. Discard the rest.

Recompute the missing segments during the backward pass. In one sentence: deliberately forget, then re-derive. The reference result (Chen et al., "Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost," arXiv:1604.06174) shows O(sqrt(n)) memory for an n-layer network. The cost is one extra forward pass per batch: roughly 33% more compute.

Step 2: the mechanics. The forward pass stores boundary activations (checkpoints). During backward, when gradients reach a checkpoint, the framework re-runs forward through the next segment to regenerate its activations, then continues backward through them. One subtlety: stochastic operations (dropout) must reproduce the same masks during recomputation, so the framework saves RNG state and replays it. A different random forward would compute gradients for the wrong function.

Step 3: the numbers. Concrete numbers from Lab 3.5. Checkpointing every 4 layers cuts activation memory 5.8x without FlashAttention: 36.24 GB to 6.24 GB. With FlashAttention it cuts 5.4x: 10.47 GB to 1.95 GB. Both cost ~33% extra compute. That ratio, ~5-6x memory for ~1.33x compute, is the number to carry into capacity planning.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Eight layer boxes in a row. Only layers 1, 4, and 8 are teal (saved); the rest are gray (discarded after forward).
  2. The dashed amber arrows are the recompute steps: during backward, each segment is re-run forward from its saved boundary to regenerate the gray boxes' activations.
  3. The price is visible: the framework computes every gray box twice (once in forward, once in recompute). The saving is visible too: only 3 of 8 layers' activations persist.

Common misunderstanding: "Checkpointing is always worth it." Below the memory wall it just slows you down 33% for nothing. It is a capacity tool: use it when activations do not fit, not as a default.

"Save every k-th layer, recompute the rest. Roughly a third more compute for five times less activation memory."

10.3 Lab 3.5: the memory-math lab

Lab 3.5: memory math (labs/lab_3_5_checkpointing.py)

Analytic accounting, not a training run: per-layer activation bytes for an illustrative transformer (L=24, d=1024, seq=2048, batch=8, heads=16, FP16), with and without FlashAttention, across checkpointing intervals. Captured output (verbatim):

Model: L=24 layers, d=1024, seq=2048, batch=8, heads=16, fp16

======================================================================
FlashAttention: OFF (attention scores materialized)
======================================================================
activation bytes per layer: 1.51 GB

strategy                     activation memory  compute
store everything                      36.24 GB  1.00x compute
checkpoint every layer                 0.81 GB  ~1.33x compute
checkpoint every 2 layers              3.42 GB  ~1.33x compute
checkpoint every 4 layers              6.24 GB  ~1.33x compute
checkpoint every 6 layers              9.19 GB  ~1.33x compute

Every-4-layers uses 5.8x less activation memory for ~33% extra compute.

======================================================================
FlashAttention: ON (no s x s matrix stored)
======================================================================
activation bytes per layer: 0.44 GB

strategy                     activation memory  compute
store everything                      10.47 GB  1.00x compute
checkpoint every layer                 0.81 GB  ~1.33x compute
checkpoint every 2 layers              1.28 GB  ~1.33x compute
checkpoint every 4 layers              1.95 GB  ~1.33x compute
checkpoint every 6 layers              2.75 GB  ~1.33x compute

Every-4-layers uses 5.4x less activation memory for ~33% extra compute.

Note the FlashAttention rows: avoiding the seq-by-seq score matrix cuts per-layer bytes from 1.51 GB to 0.44 GB before checkpointing even enters. The two techniques multiply.

Key takeaways

  • Activations, not weights, dominate training memory at depth and length.
  • Checkpointing: save every k-th layer, recompute the rest; ~1.33x compute for ~5-6x less activation memory.
  • It saves activations only: not parameters, gradients, or optimizer state.
  • Handle RNG state so recomputation reproduces the forward pass exactly.

Next: Chapter 11 hits the wall this whole volume was building toward: the fixed window, and the road to Volume 4.

Chapter 11: Bridge to Volume 4

Design prompt

  • Why can a fixed-window model not read a long document, no matter how you tune it?
  • What breaks first when sequences get long: memory, compute, or information?
  • What architecture does Volume 4 build to cross this wall?

11.1 The fixed-window wall

Step 1: the wall. A fixed-window model sees only the last W tokens. Everything before the window is not "hard to use"; it is gone. This is an information wall, not a capacity wall: no hyperparameter, no optimizer, no normalization recovers information the model never received. A bigger window is not just slower; beyond the cutoff, accuracy is chance by construction, at any speed.

Step 2: the visceral demo. Lab 3.6 makes it concrete with a copy task. Predict the last token of a sequence. The first token determines the answer.

With window W=8: sequences of length up to 8 score 100%; at length 12, 16, 24, 32 the accuracy collapses to ~50%, chance level. The target token is invisible to the window, and the model guesses. This is the cleanest possible demonstration that context limits are about information access, not model quality.

Step 3: the bridge. Everything in Volumes 1-3 assumed the relevant information is present in the input. Volume 4 builds the architecture that reads the whole sequence: attention, which lets every position look at every other position directly, removing the window entirely.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Top row (fixed window): the diagram highlights only the first 8 tiles. The rest are grayed out. The red question mark sits over the distant tile the task needs.
  2. Bottom row (full sequence): the diagram highlights every tile. The eye icon marks complete visibility.
  3. The lab numbers map directly: anything the question mark covers scores at chance. No training trick moves that mark.

"A window does not compress the past; it deletes it. What the model cannot see, it cannot learn."

11.2 The road to Volume 4

Volume 4 builds the transformer: the architecture that removes the window. Here is how each piece of this volume slots into it.

What you know                          What Volume 4 adds
======================================================================
 Ch1-2  neuron, layer, forward pass    -> the computation inside every block
 Ch3-5  loss, backprop, activations    -> how each block learns
 Ch6    optimizers (AdamW, warmup)     -> the LLM training recipe
 Ch7    normalization (pre-norm RMS)   -> the transformer block layout
 Ch8    initialization (He, small std) -> stable deep stacks at scale
 Ch9    mixed precision (BF16)         -> training that fits and flies
 Ch10   checkpointing (recompute)      -> fitting long sequences in memory
 Ch11   the fixed-window wall          -> ATTENTION: every position reads
                                         every other position. No window.
======================================================================
Volume 4: attention, transformers at scale, and the end of the window.

The through-line of this volume: a network is neurons computing z = Wx + b with kinks between layers (Chapters 1-2). Training walks the loss landscape downhill via gradients (Chapters 3-6). Training at scale is an exercise in controlling signal scale (Chapters 7-8), spending bits wisely (Chapter 9), and budgeting memory (Chapter 10). Volume 4 spends all of it on sequences without limits.

11.3 Lab 3.6: the copy task

Lab 3.6: fixed window (labs/lab_3_6_fixed_window.py)

A window of W=8 sees only the first 8 tokens; the label depends on the first token. Captured output (verbatim):

T=  4 (window sees first 8): test accuracy 100.00%   <- target inside the window
T=  8 (window sees first 8): test accuracy 100.00%   <- target inside the window
T= 12 (window sees first 8): test accuracy  54.06%   <- target INVISIBLE
T= 16 (window sees first 8): test accuracy  50.94%   <- target INVISIBLE
T= 24 (window sees first 8): test accuracy  50.31%   <- target INVISIBLE
T= 32 (window sees first 8): test accuracy  48.75%   <- target INVISIBLE

No hyperparameter fixes this. The information is not in the
input. Volume 4 builds the architecture that reads it all.
How to read this diagram.
  1. The x-axis is sequence length; the y-axis is accuracy. The shaded band marks the window (W=8).
  2. Inside the band, accuracy is 100%: the needed token is visible.
  3. Outside the band, accuracy falls to ~50% and stays there no matter how long the sequence gets. The flat chance-level line is the signature of missing information.

Key takeaways

  • A fixed window deletes the past; beyond it, accuracy is chance by construction.
  • Context limits are information limits first, speed limits second.
  • Volume 4 removes the window with attention; everything in this volume becomes the training recipe.

End of Volume 3. You now know what a network is, how it learns, and why deep ones train at all. You know neurons and kinks, gradients and optimizers, controlled scale, 16-bit arithmetic that survives, and memory traded wisely. Volume 4 puts it all to work on sequences without limits. Where to go next: Volume 4: LLM Internals, which builds attention and the transformer: the architecture that reads the whole sequence.
